sections.h2: What notice does a Massachusetts landlord have to give before filing an eviction?
sections.html:
A Massachusetts landlord has to end the tenancy with a written notice to quit before any court case can begin. The state's tenants' guide to eviction says a landlord must send this notice first, and that receiving one does not mean the tenant has to leave right away. Only a court order can force a move.

The number of days depends on the reason and on the kind of tenancy. This page covers each version, how a notice has to be delivered, and what it means for an owner who plans to sell the house.

sections.h2: How many days does each Massachusetts notice to quit give?
sections.html:
Fourteen days applies to unpaid rent, and thirty days is the usual figure for most other reasons. The table sets out the versions described by the state's court and housing pages.

SituationWritten noticeSource
Rent not paid14 days, unless the lease says otherwiseMassachusetts Court System landlord guide; G.L. c. 186, section 12
Rent not paid, federally assisted housingA 30-day notice may be usedMass.gov tenants' guide
Month-to-month tenancy at willAt least 30 days, ending at the close of a rental periodCourt System landlord guide
Lease violation or landlord wants the unit back30 daysMass.gov tenants' guide
Lease that has run outNo notice needed, since the lease sets the end dateCourt System landlord guide

The statute for a tenancy at will reads a little differently from the plain summary. It speaks of three months' notice, and when rent is paid at shorter intervals the notice must equal the gap between payment days or thirty days, whichever is longer. A gap between rent dates that runs longer than thirty days can therefore stretch the notice.

sections.h2: Can a tenant stop a 14-day nonpayment notice by paying?
sections.html:
Sometimes. Under G.L. c. 186, section 12, a tenant who has not received a similar notice in the previous twelve months keeps the tenancy by paying or tendering the full rent due within ten days after receiving the notice.

Every nonpayment notice must carry a short statement telling the tenant about this right. If the statement is missing, the tenant's time to pay stretches to the day the answer is due in a court case, though the omission does not otherwise ruin the notice. When a late payment traces back to a delay by a federal, state or municipal agency, the court must continue the hearing at least seven days and can treat the tenancy as never terminated if everything owed is tendered.

Mass.gov describes paying arrears by an agreed date as "curing" the problem. Other points it lists for nonpayment cases:

  • The RAFT program offers emergency payments of up to $7,000 per year to eligible households behind on rent.
  • A tenant with a pending RAFT application cannot be evicted, and should tell the court about it.
  • A landlord must attach a form listing rental assistance programs to a nonpayment notice.
  • A payment plan negotiated with the landlord can also stop the case from moving forward.

sections.h2: What does a valid notice to quit have to contain?
sections.html:
A valid notice names the exact day the tenancy ends and, for most reasons, states why the landlord is ending it. The Court System guide stresses that the notice exists to end the tenancy, so the tenant must actually receive it for it to work.

  • A written notice, except where a lease simply expires.
  • The specific date on which the tenancy will end.
  • The reason, when the cause is a lease violation or unpaid rent.
  • The statutory right-to-pay statement, for nonpayment.
  • The rental assistance form, for nonpayment.

No single delivery method is required. A landlord can hand the notice to the tenant, and the guide recommends having a disinterested person present. Two common shortcuts fail: a constable leaving the notice at the tenant's last usual address when the tenant never actually receives it, and a mailed notice the tenant does not pick up. Sample forms are available through the Trial Court Law Libraries, with a warning that they may not be legally sufficient in every case.

sections.h2: Why does the calendar matter, especially around February?
sections.html:
Because a month-to-month notice has to expire at the end of a rental period, the date it is served decides when the tenancy can end. The Court System guide gives one example: a notice served too late in January cannot end the tenancy by March 1, since February is shorter than thirty days.

An older notice does not always have to be repeated. A landlord who served a notice months ago generally does not need a new one, unless the right to evict was waived, for example by accepting rent in advance without a written reservation of rights, or by signing a new rental agreement that created a fresh tenancy. Owners who have taken a late rent payment since serving notice should ask an attorney whether the notice still stands.

sections.h2: What is a landlord not allowed to do while the notice runs?
sections.html:
A landlord cannot lock the tenant out, shut off services or use force to regain the home. Both the tenants' guide and the state statute say only a judge's order can remove a tenant.

Under G.L. c. 186, section 14, a landlord who willfully fails to supply water, heat, light, power or gas, interferes with quiet enjoyment, or tries to regain possession by force without judicial process faces a fine of $25 to $300 or up to six months in jail. The tenant can also recover actual and consequential damages or three months' rent, whichever is greater, plus costs and a reasonable attorney's fee.

The Court System guide adds that a landlord cannot evict for illegal reasons, such as a tenant reporting violations to health inspectors or withholding rent because of bad conditions.

sections.h2: How does a notice to quit change when the owner wants to sell the house?
sections.html:
Selling does not shorten anything. The tenants' guide says a no-fault notice to quit can be used because the landlord wants to sell the property, but it still means the landlord plans to take the tenant to court, and the case still appears on the tenant's housing record.

A sale also carries obligations that follow the tenancy. Under section 15B of the same chapter:

  • A landlord who transfers the building, whether by sale or otherwise, must pass the security deposit and its accrued interest to the new owner.
  • The new owner must tell the tenant in writing within forty-five days that the deposit was transferred.
  • If the old owner fails to transfer it, the new owner becomes liable for the deposit anyway.
  • Rent paid in advance for the last month must likewise be credited to the buyer, who must give notice within forty-five days.
  • A lease can allow the landlord to enter to show the home to a prospective purchaser.

These rules suggest that Massachusetts expects a tenancy to continue across a sale unless it is properly ended. An owner thinking of selling a rented house should ask a real estate attorney how a lease or tenancy at will carries over before listing.

sections.h2: What do owners of rented Massachusetts houses usually run into?
sections.html:
Most problems come from a notice that is late, incomplete or served in a way the tenant never actually received. A notice the tenant never actually received does not count as adequate notice under the Court System guide, which matters most when a closing date is already set.

  • Special rules apply to mobile home parks, rooming houses, dormitories, residential superintendents and public housing.
  • Government-subsidized rent may require the notice to state specific reasons, so the lease and program rules both need checking.
  • The second step after an expired notice is a summary process summons and complaint, which a constable or sheriff must serve.
  • Free mediation is available through the Community Mediation Centers, and most courts offer it as well.

Some owners choose to sell the house with the tenant still living in it. Others settle on a move-out date by agreement, which the tenants' guide describes as an option when a landlord offers a little extra time. Either route should be written down and reviewed by a lawyer.

faqs.q: How many days is a Massachusetts eviction notice?
faqs.a: It is 14 days for unpaid rent and 30 days for most other reasons, according to the Mass.gov tenants' guide. A month-to-month tenancy at will needs at least 30 days, ending at the close of a rental period, and the statute can call for more when rent dates are further apart.

faqs.q: Does a notice to quit mean the tenant has to leave?
faqs.a: No. A notice to quit is only the first step. The tenant can stay until a court orders otherwise, and a landlord cannot change the locks or remove belongings before then.

faqs.q: Can a landlord send a notice because the house is being sold?
faqs.a: Yes. Mass.gov describes this as a no-fault notice to quit. It still leads to a court case if the tenant does not leave, and the sale does not cancel the tenant's rights in the meantime.

faqs.q: Does the notice have to be mailed or hand delivered?
faqs.a: No single method is required, but the tenant must actually receive it. A notice left at an old address, or mailed and never picked up, is not adequate notice.

faqs.q: What happens to the security deposit when a rented house is sold?
faqs.a: The seller must transfer the deposit and accrued interest to the buyer, and the buyer must notify the tenant in writing within forty-five days. A buyer remains liable for the deposit even if the seller fails to transfer it.

faqs.q: Where can a tenant or owner get free help with a notice?
faqs.a: The Community Mediation Centers offer free pre-court mediation, the Court Service Centers help people without lawyers, and the Legal Resource Finder lists legal aid programs. Owners with a pending sale may also want a private real estate attorney.
